info.desc: "London Calling" is the third album by English punk rock band The Clash, released 14 December 1979, on CBS Records in the UK and in January 1980 on Epic Records in the United States. The album represented a change in The Clash's musical style, and featured elements of ska, pop, soul, rockabilly and reggae more prominently than in their previously released music. The album's subject matter included unemployment, racial conflict, drug use, and the responsibilities of adulthood. The album's cover was photographed by Pennie Smith and designed by Lowry. It was a homage to the design of Elvis Presley's debut .

podcast.body: In the summer of 1979, The Clash entered the studio to record this album with producer Guy Stevens. During a warm-up session where the band covered an old blues song by American singer Vince Taylor, Stevens secretly hit record. Despite the band's concerns that their performance was sloppy and the tempo was wrong, Stevens accepted the take, asserting that "all rock and roll speeds up." The resulting energy, as heard in tracks like "Brand New Cadillac," contrasts with modern, digitally corrected recordings. "The clash was bewildered. We can't use that. It was sloppy. The tempo was all wrong. We listened to how we speed up through the song."

podcast.body: Recorded in late summer 1979 with producer Guy Stevens, the album's tone was set by the recording of the first song, "Brand New Cadillac." Stevens' method of secretly recording warm-ups and accepting "sloppy" takes as authentic rock and roll led to a raw energy that contributed to the album's classic status. "That set the tone for the rest of London calling. And we got one of the best records in the history of rock."

podcast.body: Released just before Christmas 1979, the album features iconic artwork. The cover photo, an out-of-focus shot taken by Penny Smith on September 21, 1979, at the Palladium in New York, depicts bassist Paul Simonon trashing his instrument. Simonon was in a bad mood that night because bouncers prevented the audience from standing up and engaging with the show, leading him to destroy his bass near the end of the set. The exact time, 10:43 pm, is known because Paul broke his wristwatch while smashing his bass. The photo was accidentally taken by Smith, who was startled and didn't have time to change her Pentax camera lens. Initially embarrassed by the shot's quality, Penny was convinced by Joe Strummer the next day that he loved it and it should be the cover. The artwork's layout and typography were partly inspired by Elvis Presley's self-titled 1956 album. It has since been named the best rock and roll photo of all time and became an official British postage stamp. "At first, Penny was really embarrassed at the quality of the shot. But the next day, Joe Strummer said he loved it and that it should be the cover of the next Clash album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released on December 14, 1979, "London Calling" is a powerful double album that came after The Clash's North American tour, where they gathered new ideas and recognized the end of the punk era. The band integrated diverse genres like reggae, dub, rockabilly, calypso, garage rock, rap, and even disco, fueled by anger towards their management, record label, lawsuits, and Britain's "Winter of Discontent." Twelve of its nineteen songs were completed in just three days in August 1979. Rolling Stone named it the best album of the 1980s, solidifying its place as one of the greatest and most influential rock and roll albums of all time. "The final result was what Rolling Stone named as the best album of the 1980s. A powerful, powerful double album entitled London Calling."

podcast.body: This double album, released on December 14, 1979, featured 19 songs and marked the band's creative peak, becoming one of the most influential records ever and assuring The Clash's reputation. It expanded their sound to include Ska, Reggae, Calypso, Disco, Garage Rock, Rockabilly, and Rap, with some songs inspired by a North American tour and others by the music in the streets of Pimlico, London. Recorded over just a few days in August 1979, including 12 songs bashed out in three days, the album, originally titled "The New Testament," was produced by Guy Stevens, who prioritized feel over technical perfection. The band demanded its release as a double album, but to make it affordable for their fans, they agreed to package it like a single, lower the price, and accept a lower royalty rate.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This third album marked a significant evolution from the band's earlier fierce punk rock, incorporating diverse influences like reggae, dub, ska, blues, R&B, soul, and rockabilly. It demonstrated their readiness to discard old punk dogmas and inject new ideas to enhance their messages on racism, drug abuse, corrupt police, and unemployment, becoming known as one of the greatest rock records of all time. "The result was a third album that was unlike anything anyone could have ever expected out of that old punk rock stew. Record was called London Calling."

podcast.body: This album notably includes the song "Train in Vane" as a hidden or unlisted track. The song was quickly recorded at the end of the sessions and added to the album after a plan to give it away in a magazine fell through, resulting in its omission from the completed album artwork. "Train in Vane, the hidden or the very least unlisted track on the Clash's London Calling album."
